text: Sing Sing Correctional Facility is a maximum-security prison for men operated by the New York State Department of Corrections and Community Supervision, located in the village of Ossining, New York, United States, approximately 30 miles (48 km) north of Midtown Manhattan on the east bank of the Hudson River. It holds about 1,500 inmates as of 2019 and employed around 900 people, hosting over 5,000 visitors per month. The prison originally opened in 1826 as the fifth prison built by New York state authorities, with construction beginning in 1825 after the legislature appropriated $20,100 (roughly $559,000 in 2024) to purchase a 130-acre (53 ha) site in Mount Pleasant, near the village of Sing Sing. The name "Sing Sing" comes from the Wappinger Native American words sinck sinck, meaning 'stone upon stone,' and was formerly the name of the village. In 1970, the prison was renamed Ossining Correctional Facility, but reverted to Sing Sing in 1985. The prison property is bisected by the Metro-North Railroad's four-track Hudson Line. Sing Sing was initially considered a model prison because it turned a profit, and its early operations included a hard labor system centered on quarrying, with stones used to build notable structures like Lyndhurst mansion and Grace Church. Warden Elam Lynds implemented the Auburn system, enforcing absolute silence through whippings and other punishments. In 1844, the New York Prison Association was formed to promote humane treatment and prisoner rehabilitation, leading to Eliza Farnham being appointed to lead the women's ward at Sing Sing, where she introduced social engagement and secular literature, including novels by Charles Dickens, to the prison library. Thomas Mott Osborne, a radical reformer, served briefly as warden in 1914, criticizing traditional prison administration and writing the influential book Society and Prisons: Some Suggestions for a New Penology. After facing political opposition and being indicted, he was vindicated in court and returned to Sing Sing, where he was celebrated by inmates. Lewis Lawes served as warden from 1920 to 1941, transforming the prison into a modern facility with sports, education, and new disciplinary methods, and retired in 1941, dying six years later. In 1943, the original cellblock was closed, and its metal bars and doors were donated to the war effort. Sing Sing housed the state's execution chamber until 1963, when the last execution occurred on August 15, 1963, involving Eddie Lee Mays for murder; the final execution in New York state. A total of 614 men and women—including four under federal death sentences—were executed at Sing Sing until the abolition of the death penalty in 1972. A new Death House was built in 1920 and began executions in 1922, with high-profile cases including the Rosenbergs on June 19, 1953, and Gerhard Puff on August 12, 1954. In 1972, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in Furman v. Georgia that the death penalty was unconstitutional due to inconsistency and arbitrariness, leading to a temporary nationwide moratorium, though executions resumed in other states in 1977. The electric chair at Sing Sing was moved to Green Haven Correctional Facility in the early 1970s and never used again. In 1996, Katherine Vockins founded Rehabilitation Through the Arts (RTA) at Sing Sing, offering year-round theater workshops that improved cognitive behavior and reduced recidivism, with a formal evaluation by John Jay College for Criminal Justice showing that longer participation led to fewer inmate violations. RTA now operates at five other New York state prisons. The program was dramatized in the 2023 film Sing Sing, starring Colman Domingo and featuring real-life former inmates. Hudson Link for Higher Education in Prison, founded in 1998 by Anne Reissner through private funding after state and federal support was halted during a get-tough-on-crime campaign, provides college courses to reduce recidivism and strengthen families. In 1931, prisoners were allowed recreation opportunities, including baseball and football teams, vaudeville, and concerts, funded by ticket sales; Tim Mara sponsored the Sing Sing Black Sheep football team, providing equipment and coaching, though the program ended in 1936 when the state banned ticket sales and revenue from events, cutting off funding for prisoner families and staff. The expression "up the river" to describe someone going to prison originated in 1891 from the practice of sentencing individuals to Sing Sing, located up the Hudson River from New York City. The wardens of Sing Sing are appointed by the Commissioner of the Department of Corrections and Community Supervision. Plans to convert the original 1825 cell block into a period museum began in 2002, with local officials proposing a $5 million project linked to a retired cell block, later seeking $12.5 million in federal funding in 2007, with the museum intended to display the prison's history. The prison's coordinates are 41°9′6″N 73°52′8″W.
